item.problem_title: No outcome-blind procedure selects the time grid or the grace period
item.problem_statement: An emulated protocol has to fix three times that a randomized trial fixes in one act, when eligibility is assessed, when treatment is assigned, and when follow-up begins, and it has to fix the resolution at which time is measured, because routine data arrive as dated records rather than as scheduled visits. Clone-censor-weight and sequential emulation handle the misalignment; neither chooses the grace period or the interval width, and estimates move with both. A coarse interval lets treatment affect an outcome inside the interval before censoring applies; a fine interval produces high-dimensional nuisance models and unstable weights. Selection tools exist and use outcome information: cross-validated variance has been evaluated as a measure of data support for choosing a discretization. What does not exist is a procedure that selects either quantity from the treatment and observation proc
item.paper: Approaches to Selecting "Time Zero" in External Control Arms with Multiple Potential Entry Points: A Simulation Study of 8 Approaches.
item.evidence: Eight candidate time-zero rules are enumerated and evaluated against a known truth, and two are eliminated on performance rather than on argument, which is more than the field usually has. What is not supplied is an outcome-blind selection rule: five methods survive with bias in the Cox hazard ratio between 0.005 and 0.013 and nothing distinguishes them, so the choice is handed back to the analyst on grounds of interpretability, power and compatibility with other steps. An analyst who tries several and reports one is not detectable under this guidance.
item.quote: In selecting between the viable methods, analysts should consider the context of their analysis and justify the approach selected.

item.problem_title: Sequential emulation creates repeated participation and calendar-time confounding that its efficiency gain conceals
item.problem_statement: Sequential emulation exploits repeated eligibility: a new trial is emulated at each decision point, and a person eligible at many points contributes to many of them. The resulting within-person dependence has been addressed: clustering by person, and confidence-interval procedures for survival outcomes compared across the sandwich estimator, nonparametric bootstrap, jackknife and a linearized estimating function bootstrap, which covers better in the small-sample, low-event-rate regime that motivates the design. What has not been addressed is the calendar-time structure. Trials begun at different times occur under different treatment availability, guidelines and background risk, so a pooled estimate assumes an effect common to start times that differ in all three. item.evidence: Calendar-time confounding is measured rather than assumed away: chi-square 60.3 for the calendar contribution to treatment assignment and 137.2 for its contribution to survival, with laparoscopy adoption rising from 35 percent to 70 percent across the span. The correction offered is stratification by calendar period with cotraining so that some data-selected associations may change over time, and it moved the answer, since the unadjusted benchmark analyses differ. This addresses only the calendar-time half of the entry; the emulation enters each patient once at first colectomy, so the repeated participation that sequential designs create is not touched.

verdicts.reason: Reporting risk differences, arm-specific survival, and confidence intervals in one applied emulation is not a calibrated replication-comparison method. The quote supports descriptive comparison of outcome levels, not a prespecified estimand-aligned contrast with joint uncertainty or a rule distinguishing mismatch from sampling error.

item.problem_title: Replication is reported as a binary label rather than as a calibrated comparison of estimands
item.problem_statement: Agreement between an emulation and a trial is informative only when the estimands, populations and measurements are close enough to be comparable, and better design alignment is empirically associated with stronger concordance. The benchmarking programs report this in graded form. What is cited downstream is a binary label, usually derived from interval overlap or direction agreement, and that label discards magnitude and uncertainty and cannot diagnose why two estimates differ: two studies estimating the same quantity imprecisely agree by that criterion, and two estimating different quantities precisely disagree. No reported measure, graded or binary, separates estimand mismatch from random error, because doing so requires aligning the estimands first and then reporting a paired contrast with joint uncertainty, which no benchmarking report currently does as a matter of course.
item.paper: Temporal Trends in Clinical Evidence of 5-Year Survival Within Electronic Health Records Among Patients With Early-Stage Colon Cancer Managed With Laparoscopy-Assisted Colectomy vs Open Colectomy.
item.evidence: The comparison with the trial is carried out on the estimand scale rather than as an agreement label: the treatment effect is reported as a 5-year risk difference of minus 0.007 with an interval, and the arm-specific survival levels are compared to the trial with their own intervals, 0.074 higher for open colectomy and 0.061 higher for laparoscopy. That separates a matching contrast from a shifted level, which a binary replication verdict would hide. It does not close the entry: the headline framing is still that the emulation reached the same conclusion as the trial, and no calibration statistic or prespecified agreement margin is defined.

item.problem_title: The visit process is treated as a nuisance to be imputed rather than as part of the causal structure
item.problem_statement: Biomarkers and diagnoses are observed when a patient attends care and a clinician orders a test. That visit process depends on latent severity, on prior treatment and often on an impending outcome, so missing-at-random conditional on the recorded history can fail precisely because the recording is itself informative, last observation carried forward constructs a history in which the absence of measurement was itself evidence, and conditioning on having been observed can induce selection bias. Three estimator families now address this: multiply robust estimation under covariate-driven observation times, calibrated inverse probability weights under irregular visits, and continuous-time weights built from a marked point process. item.paper: Bias of time-varying exposure effects due to time-varying covariate measurement strategies.
item.evidence: The measurement process is drawn into the causal structure rather than left as an imputation nuisance: the observed covariate is represented as a separate node with arrows from prior and current covariates and from prior and current exposure, which makes it a collider on the path from exposure to outcome, so conditioning on it opens that path. This explains the sign flip from plus 29 percent under fixed intervals to minus 14 percent under switch-triggered measurement, and it is a genuine advance over treating gaps as missing data. What is not closed is the estimator: no method is offered that recovers the effect when measurement is exposure-driven, and the only advice is to measure more often.
item.quote: Together with LOCF, these measurement designs introduced a form of differential misclassification, which may result in bias even in the absence of confounding.

item.problem_title: Negative controls, proxies and validation data are not integrated into a standard emulation workflow
item.problem_statement: A correctly implemented emulation prevents specific design-induced temporal biases and does not create exchangeability. Active-comparator new-user designs, high-dimensional propensity scores and richer clinical measurement all reduce residual confounding without guaranteeing it. The tools that address what remains, negative control outcomes and exposures, instrumental variables, proximal causal learning and external validation samples, identify under distinct and partly untestable assumptions and sometimes target different estimands. They therefore cannot be mechanically ordered or combined: doing so requires an explicit joint model aligned to one estimand, and no such model is in use, so there is no convention for reporting what each tool contributed or for reconciling them when they disagree. item.problem_title: An unobservable protocol component produces a different, data-defined estimand rather than a noisy version of the intended one
item.problem_statement: The canonical protocol has seven linked components: eligibility, treatment strategies, assignment, follow-up, outcomes, causal contrast and analysis plan. Conceptual specification and operational realization are distinct, and when a component cannot be observed the analyst substitutes a proxy. If no valid measurement, missing-data or validation model recovers the intended variable, the resulting observed-data functional generally does not identify the intended causal effect, and it does not automatically identify some other one either: naming it a different estimand requires a corresponding intervention and an identification argument. A criterion that cannot be verified is dropped and the population changes; a strategy that cannot be distinguished from its neighbor is merged and the contrast changes; an outcome that is only partly captured redefines the endpoint. item.paper: Mediation effects that emulate a target randomised trial: Simulation-based evaluation of ill-defined interventions on multiple mediators.
item.evidence: The unobservable component here is the mediator intervention itself, and the response is not to treat the estimate as a noisy version of an intended effect but to define the data-defined estimand explicitly: shift the mediator distribution to that of the unexposed given covariates, and state the three assumptions that fix it. The resulting quantities, 0.9 percent for university completion and 1.6 percent for the joint shift, are labeled as evidence about intervention targets rather than about interventions. What remains open is that the estimand still depends on unverifiable choices, the benchmark distribution and the mediator dependence structure after intervention, so the substituted estimand is one of a family and nothing prices the distance from the intended one.

item.problem_title: No decomposition separates scientific-target mismatch from protocol compromise, mapping loss and estimation error
item.problem_statement: Three trials are in play in any emulation and only one is usually named: the ideal trial that would answer the decision-maker's question, the target trial the investigator specifies, and the emulation the data support. Specifying the target trial closely around the available data conceals the distance between the first two, and the paper reports one estimate as though the chain were tight. What is missing is not an additive decomposition; that generally does not exist, because the transitions change populations, interventions, outcomes and scales, so the discrepancies do not add. item.paper: The Target Trial: A Powerful Device Beyond Well-defined Interventions.
item.evidence: A real separation is supplied: covariates that define the estimand are shown to enter the protocol at a different component from covariates that make it identifiable, so scientific-target choices can be told apart from emulation choices by where they first appear in the table. Applied to existing mediation estimators, this shows that none of them uses covariates appropriately for the question, because they target different estimands. What it does not supply is a size for any component; the decomposition is qualitative and cannot say how much of a reported estimate is target mismatch and how much is estimation.
